subject: Staggered provisioning & warm-pool strategy for private GPU pool
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Cc: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>

Subject: Staggered provisioning & warm-pool strategy for private GPU pool

Hi Alex / Helios ops team,

Following our call yesterday, we ran a set of short simulations to evaluate two operational models for your private GPU fleet: (A) instant full-provisioning (spin-up all nodes on demand) and (B) staggered provisioning + small always-warm pool (30% hot, 70% cold with fast warm-up). The attached CSV (warmup-sim-results.csv) contains per-model latency percentiles for three traffic traces you shared.

Key ask: can you confirm your preferred failure domain for staggered provisioning (rack, AZ, or host-level)? That determines how we size the warm pool for both throughput isolation and thermal headroom.

Preliminary notes:  
- Staggered approach reduces median cold-start latency by ~40% on headroom-limited bursts versus full spin-up, at the expense of ~12% steady-state cost premium.
- Networking: we recommend enabling jumbo frames and increasing MTU to 9000 between hosts to reduce RPC stall under high-concurrency KV cache loads.
- Warm-up mechanics: two-phase KV-populate then prefix-warm; recommend a soft-traffic window of 60s pre-warm for heavy models.

Attachments: warmup-sim-results.csv, topology-diagram.png (sketch of warm-pool placement across racks).

Next steps proposed:
1) Helios confirms failure domain + preferred warm pool size (percent of fleet).
2) We run a 4-hour A/B soak in your staging VPC (Redwood will provide warmup orchestration scripts).
3) Review metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, sequential token cost) and iterate.

Thanks,
Ben

Ben — thanks for the write-up and the sim results. Quick clarifying Qs before we lock failure domain:  

1) If we pick rack-level failure domains, roughly what warm-pool fraction would you recommend for a 200-GPU private deployment to meet a sustained 4k tokens/s throughput with 99th pct latency < 450ms?
2) Do we need changes to our current network fabric (we run 25Gbps leafs and 100Gbps spines, no jumbo frames enabled right now)? Any risk to production side-effects when we flip MTU?
3) During the 4-hour soak, what guardrails do you use to avoid noisy neighbor cascades on our multi-tenant hypervisor layer?

Also looping in infra lead, Mark (ops-mark@helios.ai) on scheduling.

—Alex

On Wed, May 5, 2027 at 11:03 AM Alex Hayes <alex.hayes@helios.ai> wrote:
> Ben — thanks for the write-up and the sim results. Quick clarifying Qs before we lock failure domain:  
> 
> 1) If we pick rack-level failure domains, roughly what warm-pool fraction would you recommend for a 200-GPU private deployment to meet a sustained 4k tokens/s throughput with 99th pct latency < 450ms?
> 2) Do we need changes to our current network fabric (we run 25Gbps leafs and 100Gbps spines, no jumbo frames enabled right now)? Any risk to production side-effects when we flip MTU?
> 3) During the 4-hour soak, what guardrails do you use to avoid noisy neighbor cascades on our multi-tenant hypervisor layer?

Great questions — short answers and then an action plan.

1) Warm-pool sizing (rack failure domain): recommend 24% of GPUs warm (rounded to nearest host). For your 200-GPU example that maps to ~48 GPUs warm, spread across at least 6 racks (8 warm GPUs/rack) to keep rack-failure tolerance and avoid hotspotting. This achieves the 4k tokens/s with p99 headroom if we use 2.4x batching and KV prefix warm.

2) Network changes: enabling jumbo frames gives ~8-12% lower RPC latency under large KV churn. We do not insist on jumbo frames but we do recommend it for the soak. Risk: transient path MTU blackholes on older NIC firmware — recommend a staged rollout: enable on one leaf pair + run 24h of layer-2 path tests, then progressively enable. Our ops scripts include an MTU validation step that will rollback if packet loss >0.1% for 5 minutes.

3) Noisy neighbor guardrails during soak:
- Soft CPU/GPU cgroups throttling thresholds and QoS classing for initial 20% burst.
- Token-based admission control: new sessions are admitted into warm pool until warm KV-depth threshold reached.
- Rate-limiter enforced per-client flow on the hypervisor side (we give default conservative setting; Helios can tune).

Attachments: I uploaded the warmed simulation CSV and a topology diagram. We also added a short script to the Drive link that will pre-populate KV prefixes (link in metadata).

Proposed immediate next step: Helios confirms rack-level failure domain OK and a DST window to run the staging soak (we need a 4-hour window Monday-Thursday UTC 02:00–08:00 preferred).

Ben
